extracted.intended_audience: readers of an annotated edition of The Spectator; literary students and scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and interpreting annotated eighteenth‑century periodical essays (The Spectator) with editorial notes about authorship, text variants, and historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of speech / avoid superfluous discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of the use of speech; and the sin of superfluous discourse with regard to conversation (not religion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay illustrates the problem with examples (Mrs. Alse Copswood, Tom Bellfrey) showing people who talk too much or inappropriately. Evaluate conversational writing or characters by whether their speech is necessary and appropriate to occasion; superfluous talk is presented as a social vice and literary defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify conversational offenders by type
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect observations on various offenders: 'the whisperer without business, the laugher without wit, the complainer without receiving injuries, and a very large crowd... common impertinents whose tongues are too voluble for their brains.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing social behavior or characters, classify them into these types and judge each according to its characteristic fault (e.g., laugher without wit = empty noise; whisperer without business = feigned secrecy). The essay promises further specific observations on each kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge people in context of education and station
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove anything against the race of men, you must take them as they are adorned with education, as they live in Courts, or have received instructions in colleges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical judgment (literary or social) should account for the subject's social and educational context. Do not generalize from country manners to courtly behaviour without considering education/setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret intentional dullness as design
rubrics_metrics.description: It is to be noted, that when any part of this paper appears dull, there is a design in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and critics should not assume dull passages are failures: dullness may be a deliberate rhetorical or satirical device. Consider authorial intent and possible strategic purpose before condemning perceived dullness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public papers should instruct and divert
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of all public papers ought to be the benefit and instruction, as well as the diversion of the readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating periodical essays or public journalism, assess them on dual aims: do they both entertain and promote moral or civic instruction? Use examples in the text (pieces aimed at rooting out duelling) as models of this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial/attribution practice: look for verbal alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison's frequent practice to make verbal alterations in a preceding paper; Steele seldom did, except in rare cases or where there was a positive mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In attributing unsigned or ambiguously signed papers, examine errata lists and verbal alterations: consistent editorial habits (who revises previous numbers) are evidence for authorship attribution in this edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship clues: superscription and nature of contents
rubrics_metrics.description: All the three papers are superscribed, as Addison's often were, and appear upon the face of them, to be of the nature, and in the number of those, for which Steele stood sponsor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external markers (superscription) and the character of the contents (style, topics, tone) as criteria when deciding if a paper is Addison's, Steele's, or sponsored by one of them; where uncertain, prefer placing Steele's name per editorial convention noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republication/censorship influenced by political application
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason for cancelling this article when these papers were republished in octavo, is obvious; for, being printed by Steele, it would naturally be applied to the circumstances in which the Duke of Marlborough was at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions about including or removing material in later editions may reflect political sensitivity. When studying textual variants or omissions, consider contemporary political context as a plausible explanatory criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public writing as social reform (example: anti‑duelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writings tending to the rooting out from amongst us that unchristianlike and bloody custom of duelling; public papers can have moral effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess essays on their capacity to influence public behavior; anecdotal evidence (letter describing a quarrel resolved without bloodshed) is presented as proof of effectiveness. Value persuasive public argument that reduces social harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge a man by his intention in social conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If it be a just rule to judge of a man by his intention, according to the equity of good breeding, he that is impertinently kind or wise, to do you service, ought in return to have a proportionable place both in your affection and esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating characters or social actors, consider motive/intent as a mitigating or enhancing factor. 'Impertinently kind' persons may merit charity because their intentions are serviceable, even if results are trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat impotent malice firmly
rubrics_metrics.description: As impotent kindness is to be returned with all our abilities to oblige, so impotent malice is to be treated with all our force to depress it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text sets a normative response policy: be generous to harmless incompetence but resist and suppress useless malicious behaviour. This can inform judgments of character and prescriptions for social response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical criticism and the role of prefaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Players are grown so severe critics, that they would not take in his play, though it has as many fine things in it as any play that has been writ since the days of Dryden. He began his discourse about his play with a preface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating dramatic works and their reception, note that actors/players may act as stringent gatekeepers; a preface is often used by a playwright to frame and defend a work to such critics. Consider prefaces and contemporary theatrical tastes when appraising plays' acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character portrayal: cowardice vs heroism
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficulty grows on our sickened imagination... the coward sees the danger, and sickens under it; the hero, warmed by the difficulty, dilates, and rises in proportion to that, and in some sort makes use of his very fears to disarm it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In literary analysis of character, evaluate how characters respond to danger: effective heroic portrayal uses fear as a spur to amplified action, whereas cowardice is represented by paralysis. Use such distinctions when judging dramatic or narrative characterization.
